title: No such thing as common law marriage
subtitle: Cohabitation, the statutory vacuum, and the workarounds that fill it
objectives: State the current legal position of cohabitants on separation, and explain why 'common law marriage' is a myth with no basis in English law
Identify the workarounds cohabitants must rely on instead of a statutory scheme: TOLATA 1996 claims, proprietary estoppel, child maintenance and Schedule 1 Children Act 1989 claims
Explain the status of the government's cohabitation-reform consultation as at the check date, and why the lesson must not overstate cohabitants' current protection

leadingAuthorities.citation: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996
leadingAuthorities.role: The main property-law route cohabitants use to establish a share in the family home, in the absence of any bespoke cohabitation statute

Allows a parent to apply for capital and property provision for the benefit of a child, regardless of the parents' relationship status — the main route to housing provision for a separating cohabitant with children

Sets the framework for determining beneficial ownership of a jointly-held family home where intentions were never formally recorded — referenced here for its separation-law consequences, not its full equitable doctrine

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students arrive already believing in 'common law marriage' — because most of the public does. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can probably already state the myth-busting headline — this lesson checks whether you know exactly which statutes fill the gap, and how far each one actually reaches.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards matching a client's facts to the right claim — TOLATA, Schedule 1, or neither — rather than reciting that no scheme exists.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly. Everything else in this lesson depends on being precise about what cohabitants do NOT get before we get to what they can still claim.

overview.hook: Ask a hundred people on the street whether living together for long enough gives you the same rights as a spouse on separation, and a large majority will say yes. They are wrong, and the mistake has real consequences: a partner who spent fifteen years raising children in a house they never legally owned can walk away with nothing but a Schedule 1 claim and a lot of case law to fight through. This lesson is about the gap between what people assume the law gives them and what it actually does — and about a reform process that, as of the date this lesson is set, has changed nothing yet.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. There is NO statutory scheme giving cohabitants rights equivalent to the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 on separation, and none has been introduced. The government's 'A fairer end to relationships' consultation on statutory cohabitant protections closed on 14 August 2026; as at the check date the government has not published its response, and no bill has been introduced to Parliament. Everything in this lesson describes the law as it currently stands — a patchwork of property law, equity and child-focused statute, not a bespoke cohabitation regime. Do not treat the consultation as a change in the law: it is, at most, a signal of possible future reform.

parts.heading: The myth, and why it survives
parts.voice: argumentative — dismantles a widely-held belief before building the real law in its place
body: There is no such thing as common law marriage in England and Wales. Not a weakened version of marriage, not marriage after some number of years together, not marriage if you have children together or hold a joint mortgage. The phrase describes a status that simply does not exist in the law of England and Wales — and hasn't for well over a century.

The myth persists partly because it once had a grain of truth in very different historical circumstances, and partly because it is intuitively fair: it feels wrong that two people who have built a life, a home and a family together should end up with categorically different legal protection depending on whether they signed a register. Surveys consistently find a majority of cohabiting couples in England and Wales believe they have 'common law marriage' rights. They do not — and this misunderstanding is precisely the reason family lawyers give this area the most careful, myth-correcting treatment of anywhere in the syllabus.

The consequence is stark. On divorce, a spouse can apply for the full s 25 Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 toolkit — needs, compensation, sharing, pension sharing, spousal maintenance. On the breakdown of a cohabiting relationship, none of that exists. A cohabitant's claims, whatever they turn out to be, come from property law, equity and child law — areas built for entirely different purposes and only awkwardly adapted to this one.

components.definition: A popular but legally inaccurate belief that unmarried cohabiting couples acquire marriage-equivalent legal rights after living together for some period of time, or after having children together. No such status exists in English law; cohabitants' rights on separation depend entirely on general property law, equity and child-focused statute.

interaction.prompt: A couple have lived together for eleven years and have two children. On separation, does either partner have an automatic right to apply for the s 25 Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 financial remedies available to a divorcing spouse?
options: No — cohabitants have no access to the MCA 1973 financial remedies regime, however long the relationship lasted
Yes — eleven years of cohabitation with children triggers 'common law marriage' status
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Duration and children make no difference to this question — there is no length-of-relationship threshold that converts cohabitation into anything resembling marriage for financial-remedies purposes.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: There is no such threshold. However long a couple cohabits and whatever they build together, the MCA 1973 financial remedies regime is simply unavailable to them — that's the gap this whole lesson exists to map.

parts.heading: The first workaround: TOLATA and a share in the home
parts.voice: structural — introduces the main property-law route cohabitants actually use
body: If there is no bespoke cohabitation statute, the most-used substitute is one that was never designed with separating couples in mind at all: the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996 (TOLATA). TOLATA governs disputes about property held on trust — and a cohabitant who is not on the legal title to the family home, but claims a beneficial share in it, brings that claim under TOLATA s 14, asking the court to determine the extent of the parties' interests and, where relevant, to order a sale.

TOLATA is not a discretionary, needs-based jurisdiction the way MCA 1973 s 25 is. It answers one question: what share, if any, does each party actually own in equity? That share is fixed by ordinary trusts-of-land principles — resulting trusts, and far more commonly today, common intention constructive trusts — asking what the parties intended, expressly or by inference from their conduct, and (where title is in joint names) applying the framework in Stack v Dowden for working out what share each party holds where the parties never spelled it out.

This matters practically because TOLATA claims are frequently expensive, adversarial, and blunt: a court can find a beneficial interest exists, or find it does not, but it cannot top up an unfair result by reference to 'needs' or 'fairness' the way s 25 allows on divorce. A cohabitant who contributed unpaid domestic labour and childcare for two decades, rather than direct financial contributions to the property, may struggle to establish any beneficial share at all under ordinary trusts principles — which is exactly the gap the reform consultation discussed in Part 5 is aimed at.

components.label: What a TOLATA claim can and cannot do
points: Can determine each cohabitant's existing beneficial share in the property, based on trusts-of-law principles (resulting trust, common intention constructive trust)
Can order a sale of the property and direct how the proceeds are divided according to the shares found
Cannot redistribute property based on 'fairness' or 'needs' in the way MCA 1973 s 25 allows on divorce
Cannot award spousal-style maintenance, pension sharing, or a share of a partner's other assets unconnected to the property in dispute

interaction.prompt: Put these steps of a TOLATA dispute over the family home in the order a court actually works through them.
items: The court identifies who holds the legal title to the property
The court asks whether the non-owning or joint owner has a beneficial interest, applying trusts principles
If a beneficial interest exists, the court quantifies the share (express agreement, inference, or Stack v Dowden's approach for joint names)
The court considers whether to order a sale under s 14 TOLATA and how to divide the proceeds
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the structure: legal title first, then whether equity recognises any beneficial interest at all, then quantifying it, then the practical remedy of sale and division. Skip a step and you'll answer the wrong question in an exam.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order — you always start from the legal title, then ask whether a beneficial interest exists in equity, only then quantify the share, and only at the end reach the practical remedy of a sale under s 14.

parts.heading: The second workaround: proprietary estoppel
parts.voice: case-narrative — illustrates estoppel's role as a fallback where trusts principles fall short
body: Where a cohabitant cannot establish a beneficial interest through a common intention constructive trust — because there is no evidence the parties shared a common intention about ownership — proprietary estoppel offers a second, related route. Estoppel does not depend on the parties having agreed anything about ownership; it depends on a promise or assurance, reasonable reliance on it, and resulting detriment.

The classic pattern in a cohabitation context: one partner is assured, expressly or through a settled course of conduct, that the home (or a share of it) will be theirs; they act to their detriment in reliance on that assurance — perhaps giving up a career, a home of their own, or investing labour and money into the property — and it would then be unconscionable for the promisor to go back on the assurance. Where the elements are made out, the court has a wide discretion as to the remedy: it can order a transfer of the property, a monetary award, or a lesser interest, tailored to satisfying the equity raised rather than automatically enforcing the original promise in full.

Estoppel and TOLATA-based constructive trust claims are frequently pleaded together, in the alternative, precisely because the categories overlap and the facts of a real breakup rarely divide neatly into 'we agreed on ownership' versus 'I was promised and relied on it.' Students should be able to spot which framing a given fact pattern fits, not just recite both doctrines in the abstract.

components.definition: An equitable doctrine allowing a court to intervene where one party was assured an interest in property, relied on that assurance to their detriment, and it would be unconscionable for the assurance to be broken. Unlike a common intention constructive trust, it does not require a shared intention about ownership — only a promise, reliance and detriment — and the remedy is discretionary rather than fixed to the promised share.

interaction.prompt: A cohabitant cannot show any shared intention with her partner about who owns the house, but she gave up a well-paid job in another city and moved in after her partner repeatedly told her 'this will always be your home too.' Which claim best fits these facts?
options: A common intention constructive trust, since intention is the whole basis of the claim
Proprietary estoppel, since it turns on assurance and detrimental reliance rather than a shared intention about ownership
Neither — cohabitants outside marriage cannot bring any property claim
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Without evidence of a shared intention on ownership, a constructive trust claim is weak — but the assurance and the career-and-home sacrifice in reliance on it are exactly what proprietary estoppel is built to catch.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what's actually present in the facts: no shared intention about ownership, but a clear assurance and a costly step taken in reliance on it. That combination is the signature of proprietary estoppel, not a constructive trust.

parts.heading: Where children change the picture: Schedule 1
parts.voice: direct — moves from property doctrine to the statute most likely to actually help a separating parent
body: For a separating cohabitant with children, the most practically significant claim often isn't a property-law doctrine at all — it's Schedule 1 to the Children Act 1989, which lets a parent (or in limited circumstances a child) apply for financial provision for the benefit of a child, regardless of whether the parents were ever married.

Schedule 1 orders can include a lump sum, periodical payments (though this is now largely superseded by the child maintenance system for ongoing support), and — crucially — a settlement or transfer of property, most often used to secure housing for the child until they reach adulthood or finish full-time education. This is the route that most closely resembles a s 25 outcome for a cohabitant with children, but it is not equivalent: the provision is for the child's benefit, is typically time-limited (the property usually reverts to the paying parent once the child is grown), and there is no discretion to make an award that benefits the applicant parent in their own right once the child no longer needs it.

Ongoing routine child support — as opposed to capital provision — mostly runs through the statutory Child Maintenance Service formula rather than the courts, and sits outside this lesson's scope. What matters here is the shape of Schedule 1: real, useful, and specifically child-focused rather than any kind of substitute for a spousal financial-remedies scheme.

components.text: On an application by a parent, guardian or special guardian of a child, or by any person in whose favour a residence order is in force with respect to a child, the court may make one or more of the orders mentioned in sub-paragraph (2) below... (a) an order that either parent of the child shall make to the applicant for the benefit of the child, or to the child himself, such periodical payments... (b) an order that either parent of the child shall secure to the applicant... or to the child, such periodical payments...; (c) an order that either parent of the child shall pay to the applicant for the benefit of the child, or to the child himself, such lump sum...; (d) an order requiring a settlement to be made for the benefit of the child... of property...; (e) an order requiring a parent of a child to transfer to the applicant... or to the child, such property...
elements: Applicant must be a parent, guardian, special guardian, or person with a residence/child arrangements order
Orders are made for the benefit of the child, not the applicant parent personally
Property orders (settlement or transfer) are the closest equivalent to a s 25 outcome available to an unmarried parent
Property provision is typically structured to revert once the child no longer needs it

interaction.prompt: A separated, never-married couple have a nine-year-old daughter. The mother, who has no beneficial interest in any property, cannot afford suitable housing near the child's school. Tap the fact that makes a Schedule 1 property order realistic here, rather than a TOLATA claim.
interaction.scenarioText: The father owns the former family home outright, in his sole name. The mother never contributed to its purchase and has no TOLATA claim to any share in it. Their daughter currently lives mainly with the mother and needs stable housing near her school. The mother applies for a settlement of property under Schedule 1 for the benefit of the child.
tappableSpans: owns the former family home outright, in his sole name
never contributed to its purchase and has no TOLATA claim
needs stable housing near her school
applies for a settlement of property under Schedule 1
interaction.correctSpan: needs stable housing near her school
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the trigger. Schedule 1 doesn't depend on the applicant parent having any property claim of her own — it exists precisely because the child's housing need can be met even where the parent has no beneficial interest at all.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The key fact isn't the absence of a TOLATA claim — it's the child's ongoing housing need. Schedule 1 is triggered by what the child requires, not by whether the applicant parent has an independent property claim; the two routes address different problems.

parts.heading: A live consultation, and why this lesson must not get ahead of the law
parts.voice: reflective — closes by being explicit about what has and has not changed
body: Given how widely the current position is criticised — by family lawyers, by Law Commission reports going back decades, and by the courts themselves, which have repeatedly said reform is a matter for Parliament, not judicial invention — it should be no surprise that reform is actively being considered. In 2026 the government ran a consultation titled 'A fairer end to relationships,' seeking views on introducing a statutory scheme of financial protections for cohabitants on separation, broadly modelled on ideas the Law Commission and campaigners have floated for years.

That consultation closed on 14 August 2026. As at the date this lesson is set, the government has not published its response, and — this is the point to hold onto — no bill has been introduced to Parliament, no clause has been drafted into law, and nothing about the legal position described in Parts 1 to 4 of this lesson has changed. A consultation closing is not legislation; it is, at most, evidence that legislation might follow.

For exam purposes, and for practice, this distinction is not a technicality — it is the whole point. Stating that 'the government proposes to give cohabitants rights' as though that were current law would be a serious factual error, the equivalent of citing a bill as though it were an Act. The correct, defensible answer as at the check date is: cohabitants currently have no bespoke statutory scheme; they rely on TOLATA, estoppel, and — where there are children — Schedule 1; and a reform process is underway but has not yet produced any change in the law.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students sometimes write that 'cohabitants will soon have similar rights to spouses' or cite the consultation as though it created new statutory protections.
components.whyItsWrong: A consultation is a stage in the policy process, not legislation. As at the check date, the government has not even published its response to 'A fairer end to relationships,' let alone introduced a bill. Overstating the current legal position — even by describing likely future reform as though it were settled law — is a serious error in an exam or in practice.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that, as at the check date for this lesson, cohabitants already have a statutory right to apply for financial remedies equivalent to divorce, following the 'A fairer end to relationships' consultation?
sliderLabels: Definitely no such right exists yet
interaction.correctPosition: Definitely no such right exists yet
interaction.explanation: Correct position: no such right exists. The consultation closed 14 August 2026 with no government response published and no legislation introduced. Cohabitants remain confined to TOLATA, proprietary estoppel, and — for parents — Schedule 1 Children Act 1989.

testPool.prompt: Name the popular but legally inaccurate belief that this lesson opens by dismantling.
testPool.modelAnswer: The belief that cohabiting for long enough (with or without children) creates 'common law marriage' rights equivalent to a marriage — no such status exists in English law.

testPool.prompt: Does the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 s 25 financial remedies regime apply to separating cohabitants?
options: No — it applies only to divorcing spouses and dissolving civil partners
Yes, once a cohabiting couple has lived together for two years or more

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a claim currently available to a separating cohabitant?
options: A TOLATA claim to a beneficial share in the family home
A proprietary estoppel claim based on assurance and detrimental reliance
An application under Schedule 1, Children Act 1989 for the benefit of a child
A direct application for spousal-style maintenance under MCA 1973 s 25
testPool.trapExplanation: The first three are all genuine, currently available routes. Spousal-style maintenance under s 25 MCA 1973 is a marriage/civil-partnership-only remedy — there is no cohabitant equivalent, which is exactly the gap this lesson is about.

testPool.prompt: Put these events relating to cohabitation reform in chronological order.
items: Family lawyers and the Law Commission have long criticised the lack of a cohabitation scheme
The government opens the 'A fairer end to relationships' consultation
As at the check date, the government's response has not been published and no bill has been introduced

testPool.prompt: Under Schedule 1 Children Act 1989, what is the key limitation on a property settlement or transfer order made for a child's benefit?
options: It is typically structured so the property reverts to the paying parent once the child no longer needs it, rather than transferring outright to the applicant
It can only be made if the parents were previously married
It automatically converts into a full transfer of ownership to the applicant parent

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that most precisely distinguishes proprietary estoppel from a common intention constructive trust.
testPool.passage: A common intention constructive trust depends on the parties having formed a shared intention, express or inferred, about ownership of the property. Proprietary estoppel does not require any such shared intention; it depends instead on a promise or assurance, reasonable reliance on that assurance to the claimant's detriment, and the unconscionability of allowing the promisor to go back on it. The two doctrines are frequently pleaded together in the alternative.
testPool.ratioSentence: Proprietary estoppel does not require any such shared intention; it depends instead on a promise or assurance, reasonable reliance on that assurance to the claimant's detriment, and the unconscionability of allowing the promisor to go back on it.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most strongly supports a proprietary estoppel claim, as opposed to a straightforward constructive trust claim.
testPool.scenarioText: Priya and Sam cohabited for nine years in a house held in Sam's sole name. Priya never discussed ownership with Sam and there is no evidence either of them turned their mind to who owned the house. Sam repeatedly told Priya over the years, 'don't worry, you'll always have a home here,' and Priya turned down a job offer in another city to stay and help renovate the property.
tappableSpans: 'don't worry, you'll always have a home here,' and Priya turned down a job offer
testPool.correctSpan: 'don't worry, you'll always have a home here,' and Priya turned down a job offer
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the estoppel fact pattern in miniature: an assurance, and a real detriment (the foregone job) taken in reliance on it — without needing any shared intention about ownership.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the assurance plus the detrimental step taken in reliance on it — that combination, not the absence of a discussion about ownership, is what makes proprietary estoppel (rather than a constructive trust) the stronger claim here.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is better suited to a Schedule 1 Children Act 1989 claim rather than a TOLATA claim?
testPool.scenarioA: A cohabitant with no children seeks to establish her existing beneficial share in a jointly-titled property so the proceeds of sale can be divided.
testPool.scenarioB: A cohabitant with a six-year-old child, who has no beneficial interest in any property, needs suitable housing secured for the child until the child finishes school.
testPool.explanation: B is the Schedule 1 pattern: no existing property interest to enforce, but a child's housing need that Schedule 1 exists to address through a settlement or transfer order for the child's benefit. A is a straightforward TOLATA dispute about an existing beneficial share.

testPool.prompt: Two cohabitants separate after eighteen years together, no children, home in the sole name of one partner. The other partner made no direct financial contribution to the purchase but paid all the household bills and did substantial renovation work throughout the relationship. What is the most accurate advice?
options: There is a statutory cohabitation scheme that will divide the assets fairly regardless of legal title

The non-owning partner may have a TOLATA/constructive trust claim depending on whether the facts show a common intention as to ownership, but there is no guarantee of any share, and no discretionary 'fairness' jurisdiction equivalent to divorce
Eighteen years of cohabitation automatically confers a 50% beneficial interest
testPool.explanation: There is no bespoke scheme and no automatic threshold based on duration. The claim, if any, depends on establishing a beneficial interest under ordinary trusts-of-land principles (or estoppel) — contributions like bill-paying and renovation work are relevant evidence but do not guarantee a share the way s 25 MCA 1973 discretion would on divorce.

testPool.prompt: Wale and Deb cohabited for twelve years and have two children. The house is in Wale's sole name. Deb gave up full-time work to raise the children and never contributed to the purchase price, but has cared for both children throughout. On separation, Deb wants to know what claims she can realistically bring. Analyse her position.
factsToOrder: The house is held in Wale's sole name
Deb made no direct financial contribution to the purchase
Deb has cared for the two children throughout the relationship
Deb is seeking secure housing on separation

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Deb, an unmarried cohabitant with no financial stake in the family home, has any realistic claim on separation.
modelAnswer.rule: Cohabitants have no MCA 1973-equivalent statutory scheme. A property claim in Deb's own right would need to rest on TOLATA/constructive trust principles or proprietary estoppel, both of which are weak here absent evidence of common intention or a specific assurance. Where there are children, Schedule 1 Children Act 1989 allows an application for the child's benefit, which can include a property settlement or transfer to secure housing.
modelAnswer.application: Deb's lack of financial contribution and the absence of any stated intention about ownership make a constructive trust or estoppel claim to a personal beneficial share difficult to establish on these facts alone. However, as the resident parent of two children, Deb can apply under Schedule 1 for a property order for the children's benefit, most plausibly a settlement of the home (or alternative housing) until the children reach adulthood or finish education.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Deb's strongest realistic route is a Schedule 1 claim for the children's benefit, not a personal property claim; she should be advised clearly that there is no guarantee of a share equivalent to what a divorcing spouse would receive.

testPool.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes the legal status of the 'A fairer end to relationships' consultation as at the check date?
options: It has already been enacted as a new cohabitation statute
It is a closed consultation with no government response published and no bill introduced — the pre-existing law is unchanged
It has been formally rejected by Parliament and reform is no longer under consideration
testPool.trapExplanation: Neither extreme is correct. The consultation is neither law nor abandoned — it closed on 14 August 2026, the government's response is not yet published, and nothing has changed in the current statutory position.

testPool.prompt: Which of these two statements is the legally accurate one to write in an exam?
testPool.scenarioA: 'Cohabitants currently have no bespoke statutory financial remedies scheme on separation and must rely on TOLATA, estoppel and, for parents, Schedule 1 Children Act 1989.'
testPool.scenarioB: 'Following recent reform, cohabitants now have broadly similar rights to divorcing spouses on separation.'
testPool.explanation: A is the legally accurate, currently defensible statement. B misstates the law by treating a consultation process as though it had already produced legislation — a serious and gradeable error.

testPool.prompt: A cohabiting couple ask you, in September 2026, whether they can rely on any pending statutory reform to protect them if they separate. What is the correct advice?
options: Advise them to rely on the expected reform, since it is likely to pass soon
Advise them that no reform has been enacted, the consultation outcome is not yet published, and their position today depends entirely on existing property law, equity and (if relevant) child law
Advise them that cohabitation automatically confers spousal rights after seven years
testPool.explanation: Sound advice must be grounded in the law as it currently stands. Speculating about likely reform, or inventing a duration threshold, would both be professionally negligent and legally wrong.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states the core legal position on cohabitants' property claims.
testPool.passage: Cohabitants who are not married or civil partners have no dedicated statutory scheme for resolving finances on separation. Any claim to a share of the family home must instead be established through general property law and equity — principally the law of trusts, applied through the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996, and proprietary estoppel where the facts support it. Where there are children, Schedule 1 of the Children Act 1989 provides a separate, child-focused route to financial and property provision.
testPool.ratioSentence: Any claim to a share of the family home must instead be established through general property law and equity — principally the law of trusts, applied through the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996, and proprietary estoppel where the facts support it.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating cohabitation as a weaker version of marriage with its own sliding scale of rights. It isn't — there is no scheme at all, only general property law, equity, and child-focused statute filling the gap. The second most common mistake is describing the 'A fairer end to relationships' consultation as though it were already law.
